subject: chemistry-2
question: A laboratory water sample used in a teaching exercise contains 0.012 g of a dissolved mineral in 4 kg of solution. Expressed as parts per million by mass, what is the concentration?

options.text: 12 ppm, taking the solute mass expressed in milligrams as the ppm value
3000 ppm, using the solution mass in kilograms rather than converting it to grams
3 ppm, dividing the solute mass by the solution mass in grams and multiplying by one million
0.003 ppm, dividing the two masses in grams and multiplying by one thousand

explanation:
Parts per million by mass is (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 10^6 with both masses in the same unit: (0.012 g / 4000 g) x 10^6 = 3 ppm. Equivalently, 1 ppm by mass equals 1 mg per kg, and 12 mg / 4 kg = 3 mg/kg = 3 ppm. Choice B fails to convert 4 kg to 4000 g, and choice D applies the parts-per-thousand factor instead of parts per million. Trace concentrations are reported this way because expressing them as a percent would require awkwardly small decimals.

ELI-10: Parts per million is just a mass ratio rescaled so small numbers become readable. First put both masses in the same unit: 0.012 g of mineral in 4000 g of solution. The raw ratio is 0.000003, which is hard to read, so multiply by one million to get 3 ppm. A useful shortcut for dilute aqueous samples is that 1 ppm equals 1 mg of solute per kg of solution, so 12 mg spread through 4 kg gives 3 mg per kg, the same 3 ppm. Forgetting the kilogram-to-gram conversion inflates the answer by a factor of one thousand.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
